headline: Forget the Bunker Blitz Hype — Jones Inlet Bass Are Feeding After Dark
subhead: While the coast chases daylight blitzes, the real Jones Inlet bite is happening on bucktails after sundown, with fluke and a rebuilding weakfish run filling the daylight hours.
body_markdown:
Everybody and their brother is standing on the beach at first light this week waiting for bunker to get pushed up against the sand so the blues can turn it into a slaughterhouse. I get it — that's the sexy report right now, and it's real up in Jersey and creeping toward the bight. But that's not how you catch bass at Jones Inlet in July, and I'm not wasting my dawn patrol standing around hoping. I'm out on the rocks at Short Beach and the north jetty at Jones Inlet after the sun goes down, and that's where the fish actually are.

Here's the deal. The water's been warm right through the inlet — ocean side is sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, and the back bay and the flats off Short Beach are running warmer than that by mid-afternoon. Warm shallow water like this pushes keeper bass into a low-light and nighttime feeding pattern, and that's exactly what I'm seeing. Daytime soak sessions on the jetty rocks have been quiet — a few schoolies, nothing to write home about. But drop a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig tight to the rocks at Short Beach starting an hour before sunset, and let it sit through the tide change, and you're in business. I've had slot fish to 32 inches doing exactly that the last four nights running. Bucktail guys working white 1-ounce heads with a curly tail trailer, slow-rolled along the current seam where the inlet channel meets the flat, are connecting too — best window is the last two hours of the incoming tide right into the top, when bait gets funneled through the cut and stacked against structure.

We flagged this a week back — said that spring tide would flush the inlet hard, pulling bait out on the ebb and dragging predators in behind it on the flood. That's been the program almost to the letter. Now we're sliding into the first-quarter neap on the 21st, which means the current's going to soften up over the next few days. That's not bad news — it actually widens the bite window. When the flood isn't ripping through the cut like a fire hose, bass sit on those current edges longer instead of blowing through, and you get a longer stretch of usable water instead of one hard 45-minute window around the top of the tide.

Daytime, the fluke have been the honest bet, same as they always are here in July. Sloop Channel and the deeper cuts off the Wantagh Bridge have been holding fish in 12 to 18 feet, and the drift over the mussel bars on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the most consistent stretch. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid, dragged slow along bottom — that combo has out-produced bare bucktails two or three to one for me this week. Sizes are mixed, plenty of 15-to-17-inch fish getting tossed back, but I've had three keepers over 20 inches in the last five trips, including one just shy of five pounds working the deeper hole on the Freeport side of the channel.

Now the one I'm actually excited about — weakfish. They've been trickling back into South Oyster Bay for a couple seasons now, and this week the bite finally showed some teeth. Calm, warm evenings have been the trigger, same pattern we called out last week when things were still spotty. Working the flats off Freeport and the deeper bends in the channel behind Jones Beach with small soft plastics — 3-inch pink or chartreuse shad bodies on a light jig head — has produced weakfish in the 16-to-19-inch range right at last light and into full dark. They're not thick, and you're not going to load the cooler, but for a species that all but disappeared from this bay for a stretch of years, catching four or five in an outing on a calm night is worth getting excited about. Keep your drag light — these fish have paper mouths and you'll lose half of what you hook if you horse them.

Bluefish have been quiet right at the inlet itself, even with bunker pods reportedly moving along the beach further up the coast. If those pods funnel past Jones the way they sometimes do in late July, first light at the inlet mouth is worth a scouting run with a bucktail or a diamond jig — but I wouldn't build a whole trip around it yet. Nothing's shown here so far.

Looking ahead, I'd keep leaning on the after-dark bass bite through the neap — the softer current should stretch the productive window past what we've had on the bigger spring tides. Daytime, stick with the fluke drift in Sloop Channel and work the weakfish pattern on the next few calm evenings before any weather rolls in and stirs up the bay. If the wind stays down, this stretch has real potential to keep building.
